items.title: Jeff Dean leaves Google to found an RSI startup -- and Google is investing in it
items.idea: Demis Hassabis is stepping up to Alphabet chairman and chief scientist, with Koray Kavukcuoglu taking over all AI model development from Mountain View, reporting directly to Sundar Pichai. Separately, four of Google's most important builders, led by Jeff Dean, are leaving to found Discovery Loop, a recursive self-improvement startup -- with Google itself as an investor. The AI center of gravity shifts from London to Silicon Valley.
items.angle: Google effectively spinning out its own RSI moonshot while keeping an equity stake looks like a way to pursue the riskiest, least-governable part of the AGI race outside its own headcount and safety-review structure, while still owning the upside.
items.tweetA: Jeff Dean just left Google to start a recursive self-improvement startup -- and Google is investing in it. Translation: Alphabet doesn't want RSI on its own balance sheet or safety review. It wants the equity anyway.
items.tweetB: DeepMind's UK center of gravity just lost Hassabis to a chairman role and its top builders to a Silicon Valley spinout. Everyone obsesses over the US-China AI race. The UK-to-US one just quietly happened too.

items.title: Nvidia in talks to backstop up to $250B so OpenAI can lease its own chips
items.idea: Nvidia is shaping up as a bigger AI 'kingmaker' than ever, sitting on over $750B in resources and reportedly in talks to backstop up to $250B so OpenAI can lease its way to more compute. These deals become a pathway to recognized revenue across Nvidia's trillion-dollar-plus backlog -- Nvidia is now also acting as something like a lender of last resort to its own customer base.
items.angle: When the chip vendor is also the financier underwriting the customer's purchase of its own chips, the backlog stops being a clean demand signal and starts being balance-sheet engineering worth stress-testing.
items.tweetA: Nvidia backstopping up to $250B so OpenAI can lease Nvidia's own chips. That's not a customer, that's a vendor financing its own revenue recognition. When the lender and the seller are the same company, the backlog isn't demand -- it's balance sheet engineering.
items.tweetB: $750B+ in Nvidia resources, up to $250B earmarked to backstop OpenAI's compute leases. Nvidia's trailing revenue is under $200B. They're underwriting deals bigger than their own annual sales. Ask what happens to that backlog if OpenAI's growth disappoints.

items.title: DeepSeek -- the poster child for 'AI pricing goes to zero' -- is raising prices
items.idea: New reports that AI pricing is going to zero are overdone, per Parekh: the pricing spectrum is widening instead, cheaper at the commodity end and pricier at the frontier end. Exhibit A this week: DeepSeek told developers it plans significant price increases, while simultaneously closing an $8B funding round at a roughly $70B valuation.
items.angle: The model that broke the cheap-AI narrative in early 2025 is now the one un-breaking it -- if DeepSeek has pricing power once it reaches escape velocity, the blanket AI-deflation thesis needs a rewrite.
items.tweetA: DeepSeek -- the model that supposedly proved AI commoditizes to zero -- is raising developer prices and raising an $8B round at $70B. The 'AI is a race to the bottom' thesis just got contradicted by the company that started it.
items.tweetB: Everyone models AI pricing as one line going to zero. It's actually barbelling: commodity tier keeps falling, frontier tier -- including DeepSeek's own -- is going up. If you're long 'AI deflation kills margins' as a blanket thesis, this is the counter-data point.

items.title: Big Tech's AI talent war just flipped from comp packages to mission pitches
items.idea: US tech companies are now focused on retaining high-priced AI talent after last year's unprecedented talent grab, with mission and compounding work framed as mattering as much as pay packages.
items.angle: If comp stops being the primary retention lever after a year of nine-figure poaching wars, that's a tell the labor arms race is cooling -- worth watching against hyperscaler opex-growth assumptions, since AI-talent comp inflation has been a real cost input.
items.tweetA: Last year: nine-figure pay packages to poach AI researchers. This year: tech companies selling mission over money. That's not altruism, that's the labor bidding war running out of ammo -- watch AI-related opex growth decelerate alongside it.
items.tweetB: The AI talent war shifted from 'who pays more' to 'who has the better mission story' in about 12 months. Comp curves don't reverse that fast unless the war is actually cooling -- a labor-cost tailwind nobody's pricing into hyperscaler margins yet.

items.title: SpaceX spending $2 for every $1 of revenue -- and ~$120B of stock unlocks within days
items.idea: SpaceX's first quarterly report since its AI-linked IPO showed revenue up 92%, spending running at roughly twice revenue, and management reasserting a $100B ARR target for year end. The market is now watching a roughly 900 million share lockup -- over $120B at current valuations -- lifting within days.
items.angle: Spend outpacing revenue 2:1 while reiterating an aggressive ARR target is a classic set-up right before a massive supply event -- the lockup, not the fundamentals, is probably the near-term price driver.
items.tweetA: SpaceX spending $2 for every $1 of revenue and still guiding to $100B ARR by year end. Meanwhile ~$120B of stock unlocks within days. The fundamentals debate is a distraction from what actually moves the price this week: pure share supply.
items.tweetB: 92% revenue growth sounds great until spend is growing twice as fast. Fine if you're building capacity ahead of demand -- a problem if the $100B ARR target slips right as 900 million newly-unlocked shares go looking for an exit.

items.title: US students and faculty are turning more positive on AI in the classroom
items.idea: Parekh flags a sentiment shift: US students and faculty are trending more positive on AI adoption, a turn after years of academic-integrity panic over LLMs in coursework.
items.angle: Education is usually one of the slowest, most change-averse institutions to adopt new tech -- when the holdouts start warming up, it reads as late-cycle confirmation of adoption elsewhere rather than an early signal.
items.tweetA: US faculty went from banning ChatGPT in syllabi to warming up to it. Education is typically the slowest adopter of new tech in any institution -- when the holdouts flip, that's usually late-cycle confirmation, not an early signal.
items.tweetB: Watch education sentiment as a proxy for institutional AI adoption generally. If the most change-averse profession in America -- tenured faculty -- is coming around, the harder adoption fights in healthcare, government and legal get easier to win by comparison.

items.title: White House's new AI Framework reportedly leaves US open-source models alone -- for now
items.idea: Parekh notes the White House's new AI Framework leaves US open source untouched for the time being, even as broader federal AI rules get formalized -- a bifurcated approach that spares the open-weight ecosystem while presumably tightening around frontier closed labs.
items.angle: If compliance costs land on frontier labs while open weights stay unregulated, that is a structural cost advantage for open-source players and whoever fine-tunes on top of them, versus OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
items.tweetA: White House AI framework reportedly carves out an exemption for open-source models. If compliance costs land only on frontier labs, that's a de facto subsidy for Llama-style open weights -- regulation as competitive moat, pointed the opposite way most people expected.
items.tweetB: Everyone assumed AI regulation would entrench incumbents with compliance-cost moats. The current draft does the opposite for open source. Worth tracking whether that survives the next 'AI framework' revision, because right now it's a gift to the open-weight ecosystem.

items.source: Stephen Innes (Dark Side of the Boom)
items.title: The most dangerous moment in trading isn't a losing streak -- it's a winning one
items.idea: Innes argues traders get far less forensic scrutiny during winning streaks than losing ones -- nobody spends the evening after a huge day asking whether the market simply handed them the money. That asymmetry lets confidence, and then size, creep up right as a winning streak's underlying regime is most likely to be about to shift, which is exactly when the 'hot hand' framing becomes dangerous.
items.angle: This maps directly onto the current multi-year mega-cap AI trade: almost nobody is doing the forensic post-mortem on the winners to separate genuine stock-picking edge from simply being long a favorable regime (Fed liquidity plus the AI capex boom), and position sizing hasn't been stress-tested for what happens when that regime turns.
items.tweetA: Every AI-momentum trader right now is living the setup Innes describes: a streak long enough to start feeling earned. Nobody does the forensic post-mortem on the winners, only the losers. That asymmetry is exactly how max size ends up on the table right as the regime turns.
items.tweetB: The 'hot hand' fallacy isn't just a poker thing -- it's the entire mega-cap AI trade right now. Three years of being right about Nvidia and the hyperscalers doesn't mean you've developed edge; it might just mean you're long the regime. Worth asking which one it is before adding size here.
